etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English *bangen, from Old English *bangian or borrowed from Old Norse banga (“to pound, hammer”); both from Proto-Germanic *bangōną (“to beat, pound”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰen- (“to beat, hit, injure”). Cognate with Scots bang, bung (“to strike, bang, hurl, thrash, offend”), Icelandic banga (“to pound, hammer”), Old Swedish bånga ("to hammer"; whence modern Swedish banka (“to knock, pound, bang”)), Danish banke (“to beat”), bengel (“club”), Low German bangen, bangeln (“to strike, beat”), West Frisian bingel, bongel, Dutch bengel (“bell; rascal”), German Bengel (“club”), bungen (“to throb, pulsate”).

In the sense of a fringe of hair, from bang off.

In the sense of abrupt left turn, from Boston left and associated risk of a crash.

definitions.definition: A sudden percussive noise.

quote.citation: 1992, Bob Magor, Blood on the Board, page 39:
quote.text: A fiendish yell then followed / Ev'ry salvo's 'bang' and 'bloop'.

definitions.definition: A strike upon an object causing such a noise.
An explosion.
(US, archaic) Synonym of bangs: hair hanging over the forehead, especially a hairstyle with such hair cut straight across.

quote.citation: 1880, William Dean Howells, The Undiscovered Country:
quote.text: his hair cut in front like a young lady's bang

quote.citation: 1902, Barbara Baynton, Squeaker's Mate; reprinted in Carmel Bird, editor, The Penguin Century of Australian Stories, 2000, →ISBN:
quote.text: She was not much to look at. Her red hair hung in an uncurled bang over her forehead

definitions.definition: (chiefly US) The symbol !, known as an exclamation point.

quote.citation: 1980, C.W. Wilkinson, Peter H. Clarke, Dorothy C.M. Wilkinson, Communicating through Letters and Reports, 7th edition, page 651:
quote.text: Incidentally, a useful abbreviation for "Exclamation point" is "Bang."

definitions.definition: (mathematics) A factorial, in mathematics, because the factorial of n is often written as n!
(vulgar, slang) An act of sexual intercourse.
An offbeat figure typical of reggae songs and played on guitar and piano.
(slang, mining) An explosive product.
(slang) An injection, a shot (of a narcotic drug). [from 20th c.]

quote.citation: 1951 December 20, William S. Burroughs, “To Allen Ginsberg”, in Oliver Harris, editor, The Letters of William S. Burroughs, 1945–1959, New York: Penguin, published 1993, →ISBN, page 98:
quote.text: Of course, I take a bang or some mud in coffee now and then, and I pick up on gage right smart.

quote.citation: 1952 January 19, William S. Burroughs, “To Allen Ginsberg”, in Oliver Harris, editor, The Letters of William S. Burroughs, 1945–1959, New York: Penguin, published 1993, →ISBN, page 101:
quote.text: As for myself, I take a bang now and then—I know plenty of croakers—but I really couldn't keep up a habit without a lot of running around and bother.

definitions.definition: (slang, US, Boston area) An abrupt left turn.
(Ireland, colloquial, slang) strong smell (of)
(slang) A thrill.

quote.citation: 1951, J. D. Salinger, The Catcher in the Rye, Boston, Mass.: Little, Brown and Company, →OCLC, page 38:
quote.text: I hate the movies like poison, but I get a bang imitating them.

quote.citation: 1993, Douglas Woolf, Sandra Braman, Hypocritic Days & Other Tales, page 40:
quote.text: "We all know you give great parties, Mr. Lippincott.""It gives me a bang, even a bigger bang than this," Mr. Lippincott said, indicating his drink and then finishing it.

quote.citation: 2000, James Hadley Chase, Make the Corpse Walk, page 31:
quote.text: Yes, he got a bang out of cheating Rollo.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To make sudden loud noises, and often repeatedly, especially by exploding or hitting something.
(transitive, intransitive) To hit hard.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Othello, the Moore of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act II, scene i]:
quote.text: The desperate tempest hath so banged the Turks.

quote.citation: 1922, Michael Arlen, “3/19/2”, in “Piracy”: A Romantic Chronicle of These Days:
quote.text: Ivor had acquired more than a mile of fishing rights with the house; he was not at all a good fisherman, but one must do something; one generally, however, banged a ball with a squash-racket against a wall.

definitions.definition: (slang, transitive, intransitive, vulgar) To engage in sexual intercourse.

quote.citation: 1996, Cameron Crowe, Jerry Maguire, spoken by Bob Sugar (Jay Mohr), Culver City, Calif.: TriStar Pictures; distributed by Columbia TriStar Home Video, published 1997, →ISBN:
quote.text: It's also my job to take care of the skanks on the road that you bang.

quote.citation: 1972, Mario Puzo, Francis Ford Coppola, The Godfather:
quote.text: Moe Greene: He was banging cocktail waitresses two at a time!

definitions.definition: (with "in") To hammer or to hit anything hard.
(transitive) To cut squarely across, as the tail of a horse, or a person's forelock; to cut (the hair).

quote.citation: c. 1883, Frank Hamilton Cushing, Becomin a Zuni:
quote.text: His hair banged even with his eyebrows.

definitions.definition: (transitive, slang, drugs) To inject intravenously.
(finance, transitive, dated) To depress the prices in (a market).

quote.citation: 1821, Bank of England, The Bank - The Stock Exchange - The Bankers ..., page 64:
quote.text: This accompt has been made to appear a bull accompt, i.e. that the bulls cannot take their stock. The fact is the reverse; it is a bear accompt, but the bears, unable to deliver their stock, have conjointly banged the market, and pocketed the tickets, to defeat the rise and loss that would have ensued to them by their buying on a rising price on the accompt day  […]

quote.citation: 1902, Truth, volume 50, page 1138:
quote.text: […]  the London "Bears" have promptly banged the market again  […]

definitions.definition: (slang, transitive, obsolete) To excel or surpass.
(intransitive, stative, slang) To be excellent; to be banging
(Nigeria, slang) To fail, especially an exam; to flunk.
(New England, slang, intransitive) To make a turn in a vehicle; to hang a right, left, or uey.
(US, slang) Shortened form of gangbang, to participate in street gang criminal activity.
Right, directly.

quote.citation: 2011 September 18, Ben Dirs, “Rugby World Cup 2011: England 41-10 Georgia”, in BBC Sport‎[1]:
quote.text: After yet another missed penalty by Kvirikashvili from bang in front of the posts, England scored again, centre Tuilagi flying into the line and touching down under the bar.

definitions.definition: Precisely.
With a sudden impact.
A sudden percussive sound, such as made by the firing of a gun, slamming of a door, etc.

quote.citation: 1886 October – 1887 January, H[enry] Rider Haggard, She: A History of Adventure, London: Longmans, Green, and Co., published 1887, →OCLC:
quote.text: Bang! Away he goes with a mighty bound. Leo has missed him. Bang! right under him again. Now for a shot. I must have one, though he is going like an arrow, and a hundred yards away and more.

quote.citation: 1898, H.G. Wells, The War of the Worlds, London: William Heinemann, page 84:
quote.text: “Just like parade it had been a minute before then stumble, bang, swish! Wiped out!” he said.

quote.citation: 1899 February, Joseph Conrad, “The Heart of Darkness”, in Blackwood’s Edinburgh Magazine, volume CLXV, number M, New York, N.Y.: The Leonard Scott Publishing Company, […], →OCLC, part I, page 215:
quote.text: Serve him right. Transgression—punishment—bang! Pitiless, pitiless.

quote.citation: 1956, Anthony Burgess, Time for a Tiger (The Malayan Trilogy), published 1972, page 17:
quote.text: We help to kill the bloody bandits. Bang, bang, bang.

definitions.definition: Alternative form of bhang (“cannabis”)
